dc_moratorium.why: Statements favor building AI infrastructure and note power costs as a constraint (s8) and describe unions rebutting a data center backlash (s7), but none addresses a moratorium on data centers.

dc_ratepayers.why: s8 treats rising power costs as a constraint on building but says nothing about who should pay for grid upgrades.

layoff_reporting.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

bias_audits.why: General deregulatory and growth statements (s1, s11, s26) do not address bias audits or discriminatory AI.

training_consent.why: s6 and s14 condemn foreign misappropriation of American IP but do not call for a consent, payment, or training-data disclosure rule for AI developers.

preemption.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

chips.why: s10 concerns outbound investment screening, and s20-s24 concern China's export controls on rare earths; neither addresses U.S. export controls on AI chips or chip-making tools.

testing_mandate.why: s31 refers vaguely to working on safety and s26 to slashing regulations, but no statement addresses mandatory pre-release safety testing or audits.

transparency.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

whistleblowers.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

liability.why: Bessent said the wrong thing to do on safety is give AI labs the liability exemption they are asking for, supporting developer liability rather than a shield.

misuse.why: s33 discusses using frontier AI for cybersecurity defense, not rules on AI weapons or WMD-related safeguards.

nuclear.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

autonomous_weapons.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

licensing.why: General statements about optimizing regulation and slashing harmful regulations (s1, s11, s26) do not name AI licensing or a new AI agency.

intl_agreement.why: s2, s9, and s16 reference international AI growth and economic discussions, not a safety treaty or formal risk agreement.

pause.why: s34 stresses the stakes of falling behind on AI but does not address a pause, moratorium, or compute limits.

rsi.why: No stance in the supplied evidence.

superintelligence.why: s34 implies a competitive urgency about AI leadership but does not address a ban on superintelligence.

statements.text: Economic security – the condition of having secure and resilient domestic production capacity – is core to financial stability, and leadership in AI adoption is a crucial component of economic security,” said U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We are optimizing regulation to support growth for both Main Street and Wall Street: moving from a posture focused on constraint toward one that recognizes failure to adopt productivity-enhancing technology as its own risk.

statements.text: The proposed regulations would strengthen the existing Outbound Investment Security Program to prevent our adversaries from using U.S. investment to develop critical technologies that threaten U.S. national security. This important step also helps promote our commitment to an open investment environment by providing clarity to U.S. and foreign investors as well as an opportunity for them to provide feedback on the proposed regulations.

statements.text: We are optimizing regulation to support growth for both Main Street and Wall Street: moving from a posture focused on constraint toward one that recognizes failure to adopt productivity-enhancing technology as its own risk. The Treasury Department will continue evaluating regulatory frameworks and enforcement policies to enable the U.S. financial sector’s leadership in AI adoption while preserving national security and long-term economic resilience.
